entries.reason: the question is whether the compose controller this release has can carry a subject at all, and that is answered off the controller's own metadata rather than off a constant: -setSubject: arrived in iOS 7
entries.effect: YES exactly when the release's own MFMessageComposeViewController has -setSubject:, NO on this release, whose class carries -recipients, -setRecipients:, -body, -setBody: and -messageComposeDelegate and no subject accessor at all (measured in the armv7 6.1.3 cache's ObjC metadata)
entries.source: the headers of MFMessageComposeViewController.h in SDK 26.2 for the contract; the release's own armv7 6.1.3 ObjC metadata read by objc.binary_inventory

entries.reason: the same question for attachments, read off the same metadata: -addAttachmentData:typeIdentifier:filename: arrived in iOS 7, and a controller without it has no row to put an attachment into
entries.effect: YES exactly when the release's own controller has -addAttachmentData:typeIdentifier:filename:, NO on this release - and NO is the truth here, since iOS 6's Messages sends a text message and has no attachment path to send anything else with
entries.source: the header of MFMessageComposeViewController.h in SDK 26.2; the release's own armv7 6.1.3 ObjC metadata

entries.reason: two questions, both answered from the release rather than from a table in this file: whether the controller can carry an attachment at all, and whether the release's own type store knows the identifier
entries.effect: NO on this release, because +canSendAttachments is NO. Where a release's controller does have the attachment methods, the second half is UTTypeConformsTo against public.data, which answers for an identifier the release's MobileCoreServices store holds a record for and not for one it does not
entries.source: the header of MFMessageComposeViewController.h in SDK 26.2; UTTypeConformsTo is public from iOS 3 to 14 in MobileCoreServices

entries.reason: the header's own answer for an attachment the composer will not take is NO, and this release's composer will not take one; the call records what it was given so -attachments can report it truthfully rather than dropping it
entries.effect: NO on this release, for both of the reasons -attachments reports: +canSendAttachments is NO, and the release exports neither of the array's two key constants, checked through dlsym at the moment of the call. NO for a nil URL. Where a release has both, the URL is recorded under the alternate filename, or under the URL's last path component, and -attachments answers with it
entries.source: the header of MFMessageComposeViewController.h in SDK 26.2; the release's own armv7 6.1.3 ObjC metadata

entries.reason: the same seam and the same contract as the URL form, with the type the header asks for checked first
entries.effect: the same two reasons as the URL form, and the type +isSupportedAttachmentUTI: rejects is a third; where a release has both keys, the data is recorded under the filename and -attachments answers with it

entries.reason: the property reports what the controller holds, and holding nothing is what this release's composer can do - the report is the truth about the controller, not a placeholder
entries.effect: an empty array on this release, for two independent reasons: both add methods answer NO because the release's composer has no attachment row, and the two keys of each dictionary are the release's own MFMessageComposeViewControllerAttachmentURL and MFMessageComposeViewControllerAttachmentAlternateFilename constants, which this release does not export at all (absent from the armv7 6.1.3 cache's symbol table, measured with dump-cache.lua), so nothing could be read back out of a dictionary the port invented the keys for. Where a release has both, each attachment is one dictionary under the release's own key strings

entries.reason: the API asks for the address the sender would rather send from, and the release's mail composer has the one field that means it: the To: field, which the user may still edit - the property is a preference, not a lock
entries.effect: puts the address in the To: field, through the release's own -setToRecipients:, so the composer shows it and the sender can change it; a nil or empty address clears the field, which is what the header's nullable says
entries.source: the header of MFMailComposeViewController.h in SDK 26.2; the release's own armv7 6.1.3 ObjC metadata carries -setToRecipients: on MFMailComposeViewController

entries.reason: the completion reports whether the provider was inserted, and this release's mail composer has no collaboration row to insert one into, so NO is the answer rather than a silence
entries.effect: calls the completion handler with NO on the calling thread, and says so once in the log the first time it is called
entries.source: the header of MFMailComposeViewController.h in SDK 26.2

entries.reason: Apple's own abstract for it is one line - 'This property sets the initial interactive message' - so it is a value property: the message given is the message read back, and the message itself is a class the port now carries (registry/Messages/ios10.json)
entries.effect: copied in and copied out. Reading it before anything was set answers a fresh MSMessage carrying the body the release's own composer holds, not nil. What the release cannot do is make that message interactive: iOS 6.1.3's Messages sends a text message and has no iMessage, no interactive bubble and no URL payload, and the release's own MFMessageComposeViewController has no notion of a message at all (measured in its armv7 6.1.3 ObjC metadata), so the session, URL, layout and captions travel with the message and are never drawn; the same truth +canSendSubject and +canSendAttachments report
entries.source: the header of MFMessageComposeViewController.h in SDK 26.2 for the contract; the port's own MSMessage (registry/Messages/ios10.json); the release's own armv7 6.1.3 ObjC metadata for the composer, which has no message surface
